topics.title: Flow of control, if and if-else

learn.hook: An ATM doesn't give cash to everyone. It checks: is the PIN right? Is there enough balance? Every check is an if.
points: Flow of control is the order in which statements of a program are executed.
Three structures: sequential (statements one after another), selection/conditional (choose a path using a condition) and iteration/repetition (repeat statements in a loop).
if statement: if condition: followed by an indented block. The block runs only when the condition is True; otherwise it is skipped.
if-else: if condition: block1 else: block2. Exactly one of the two blocks runs. The colon (:) after if and else is compulsory.
Flowchart: a decision diamond with a True path leading to the if-block and a False path leading to the else-block (or past the if-block).

example.q: Write a program that prints 'Eligible' if age is 18 or more, else 'Not eligible'.
steps: For age 17 → Not eligible; age 18 → Eligible
example.answer: Uses if-else with the condition age >= 18

topics.title: elif ladders, nested if and indentation

learn.hook: Grades A, B, C, D, E… Instead of five separate ifs, Python gives you a ladder: if, elif, elif, else.
points: if-elif-else ladder: conditions are checked from top to bottom; the FIRST True condition's block runs and the rest are skipped. else (optional) runs if none is True.
Because checking stops at the first True condition, the order of conditions matters: check marks >= 90 before marks >= 75.
Nested if: an if (or if-else) placed inside another if's block, for decisions that depend on earlier decisions.
Indentation (leading spaces, usually 4) marks which statements belong to a block. All statements in a block must have the same indentation.
Inconsistent or missing indentation gives IndentationError (a kind of syntax error).

example.q: Find the grade for marks = 82 using: >= 90 'A', >= 75 'B', >= 60 'C', else 'D'.

learn.hook: With just if-elif-else you can already build a calculator, a grade card and a leap-year checker. Let's code them.
points: Absolute value: if n < 0: n = -n. Larger of two: if a > b: print(a) else: print(b).

learn.hook: Printing a table of 7 with ten print statements is boring. A for loop does it in two lines, for any number.
points: Loops repeat a set of statements, so we don't write the same code again and again.
for variable in sequence: runs the block once for each item of the sequence (a string, list, tuple or range), in order.
range(stop) gives 0 to stop − 1. range(start, stop) gives start to stop − 1. range(start, stop, step) moves by step. The stop value is never included.
Negative step counts down: range(10, 0, −2) gives 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. If the range is empty (e.g. range(5, 1)), the loop body doesn't run.
Programs: print 1 to n; even numbers with range(2, n + 1, 2); multiplication table: for i in range(1, 11): print(n, 'x', i, '=', n * i); sum of first n numbers with total += i.

learn.hook: You don't know how many digits a number has, so you can't use a fixed range. A while loop keeps going until the job is done.
points: while condition: repeats its block as long as the condition is True. The condition is checked before every iteration; if it is False at the start, the block never runs.
A while loop needs: (1) a loop variable initialised before the loop, (2) a condition using it, (3) an update inside the loop that moves it towards making the condition False.
If the update is missing or wrong, the condition never becomes False: an infinite loop. e.g. i = 1; while i <= 5: print(i) (no i += 1).
Digit programs use n % 10 to get the last digit and n // 10 to remove it: sum of digits, reverse a number (rev = rev * 10 + digit).
Factorial: f = 1; while n > 1: f *= n; n −= 1. HCF by Euclid: while b != 0: a, b = b, a % b, then a is the HCF.

example.q: Reverse the number 472 using a while loop.

topics.title: break, continue, pass and loop else

learn.hook: Searching for your roll number in a list of 500? Once you find it, stop. That's break.
points: break immediately exits the innermost loop; control goes to the first statement after the loop.
continue skips the rest of the current iteration and jumps to the next iteration of the loop.
A loop can have an else clause. It runs when the loop finishes normally (condition becomes False or the sequence ends), but NOT if the loop was ended by break.
pass does nothing. It is a placeholder where a statement is required by syntax but no action is needed yet, e.g. an empty if-block.
Prime check with break: for i in range(2, n): if n % i == 0: print('Not prime'); break — else: print('Prime'). The loop's else runs only if no divisor was found.

steps: Because of break, the loop's else does not run

learn.hook: A clock's minute hand goes round 60 times for every turn of the hour hand. That's a nested loop.
points: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For every single iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely.
Total inner iterations = outer count × inner count (when the inner range is fixed). e.g. for i in range(3): for j in range(4) → 12 runs.
Patterns: the outer loop controls rows; the inner loop controls what is printed in each row. Use print(..., end='') inside and print() after the inner loop to move to the next line.
Primes in a range: an outer loop over numbers and an inner loop over possible divisors (with break and loop else).
Series like 1 + x + x² + … + xⁿ: loop i from 0 to n, add x ** i. Exam tasks: predict output, convert a for loop to while, count iterations.

Assertion (A): In a nested loop, the inner loop completes all its iterations for each iteration of the outer loop.
Reason (R): The inner loop is part of the body of the outer loop.
options: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
quiz.explain: Since the inner loop sits in the outer loop's body, it runs fully every time the body runs.
steps: A: the inner loop completes all its iterations for each outer iteration — true
R: the inner loop is part of the outer loop's body — true, and that is why it runs fully every time
Answer: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks the loops take turns one step each

teach.ask: Gappu wants to print a triangle of stars. Explain nested loops and how they make patterns.
teach.praise: The outer loop handles rows, and the inner loop prints each row's stars, completing fully every time. Triangle done!

revise.summary: In a nested loop, the inner loop runs completely for every iteration of the outer loop, so total inner runs = outer count × inner count. In patterns the outer loop controls rows and the inner loop the content of each row; print() after the inner loop moves to a new line.
